summary: We developed an app for children to spark curiosity for space exploration and teach about hardware used in space history. We want to inspire the engineers of tomorrow, by offering a story driven game that teaches playful facts about hardware that is abandoned. Is has active interactions, some quiz, minigames and more. All the hardware has some character to tell some emotional stories that stay better in mind
details:
Our project is a child-friendly mobile app built in Unity that transforms NASA’s discarded space equipment into an interactive mini-game experience. Instead of viewing old satellites, probes, and hardware as forgotten junk, we reimagine them as characters and tools in a story-driven adventure designed for young players aged 5 to 10.

How it works: Players explore a colorful space environment where they encounter pieces of real NASA equipment that have been left behind in orbit or on other planets. Each object has a name, a backstory, and a small mini-game attached to it - turning learning about space history into something playful and memorable. A child might fix a broken antenna on the Hubble Space Telescope or help a lonely Mars rover find its way home.

Benefits and impact: The app makes space history accessible and emotionally engaging for children who would otherwise never interact with this content. By giving discarded equipment a voice and a story, we hope to inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers, and storytellers. The project also raises awareness about space debris and the lifecycle of space missions in a way that feels natural and age-appropriate rather than overwhelming.

Tools and technology: We developed the project using Unity as our primary game engine, with C# for all gameplay programming. AI tools supported our development process - helping us write and iterate on code faster, generate concept art and character ideas, and refine our storytelling approach. Our team of two worked with a clear division of roles: one focused on narrative design and story writing, the other on programming and technical implementation.

Creativity and team considerations: Our main creative decision was to give inanimate, forgotten objects a personality and an emotional arc. Rather than presenting NASA’s equipment as data points, we treated each piece as a character with its own history and feelings. We considered our young target audience throughout every decision - keeping the language simple, the visuals engaging, and the mini-games short and rewarding. We also thought carefully about accessibility, making sure the app works without prior knowledge of space science.
